Authentication asks “Who are you?” Authorisation asks “May you do this?” A password is not a token and a token should not be treated like public text.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Follow the complete Identity flow

ASP.NET Core Identity stores hashed passwords and user records through Microsoft.AspNetCore.Identity.EntityFrameworkCore. AddIdentityApiEndpoints registers its API authentication services. AddEntityFrameworkStores connects Identity to AppDb. MapIdentityApi under /auth maps registration, login and other account endpoints. This example uses Identity’s opaque bearer tokens; they are not JWTs. 

POST http://localhost:5100/auth/register
Content-Type: application/json

{"email":"student@example.com","password":"ChooseYourOwn_Strong123!"}

POST http://localhost:5100/auth/login?useCookies=false
Content-Type: application/json

{"email":"student@example.com","password":"ChooseYourOwn_Strong123!"}

Use the response

Register returns 200 with no useful resource body when successful. Login returns accessToken, refreshToken, tokenType and expiry information. Copy the actual accessToken into the token variable in requests.http. Then send Authorization: Bearer followed by the token when calling /api/students. Wrong credentials should return 401. Never commit your real token. Use /auth/refresh with the refresh token for the supported refresh flow.

Before a real deployment

  • Serve authentication over HTTPS. Local HTTP in this lab is restricted to localhost experiments.
  • Configure confirmed email, delivery, password-reset and account recovery before relying on account verification. The sample does not send emails.
  • For a browser-first application consider secure HttpOnly cookies with CSRF protection instead of storing bearer tokens in localStorage.
  • For enterprise SSO, third-party clients or JWT/OAuth requirements use a real OpenID Connect/OAuth provider and validate issuer, audience, signature and lifetime. Do not invent your own token format or password encryption.
  • 401 means not authenticated; 403 means authenticated but lacking permission. Add roles/policies for staff/admin functions, not a client-side role dropdown.

Try it yourself

Can you decode this opaque token as a JWT?

Worked answer

No. This Identity flow issues a proprietary protected token. Do not promise JWT claims or third-party JWT interoperability.

How do you prove ownership isolation?

Worked answer

Register two test accounts, create a row under the first, then try GET/PUT/DELETE of that ID under the second. Expect no access to the first account’s row.
